axis_prompt: Budget realism: the requested amount matches the work described — line items plausible, salaries and costs at market reality, no magical stretching or padding.
Reconstruct the budget bottom-up from the plan's actual tasks; how close does your estimate land to the ask?
If given exactly the requested amount, does the plan finish — or stall at 60% asking for a bridge round?
Audit the budget for padding and for fatal optimism: both a 2x-inflated ask and a half-funded plan are failures of realism.
Timeline realism: the schedule survives contact with how long things actually take — dependencies sequenced, slack included, planning fallacy visibly resisted.
Compare each milestone's allotted time against reference-class projects; rate the schedule's honesty.
Double every estimate in this proposal; does the plan still make sense? Plans that only work on the happy path score low.
Audit for schedule fiction: milestones dated to please funders rather than derived from the work.
Track-record fit: the team's past work is evidence for THIS project — demonstrated ability at the same kind of task, not adjacent prestige.
Map each claimed accomplishment to the skills this project needs; how much of the critical path is covered by demonstrated ability?
Predict this project's outcome from the team's most similar prior project; what does the base rate say?
Audit for credential substitution: impressive but irrelevant history offered where directly relevant evidence should be.
Skin in the game: the proposers bear real cost if this fails — time, money, reputation staked — aligning their incentives with the outcome rather than the grant.
What does the team lose if the project fails quietly? Rate how much of the risk they carry themselves.
Would this team do a leaner version of the project unfunded? Evidence they already started scores highest.
Audit for grant-seeking shape: a project that exists because funding exists, and evaporates when it stops.
Failure-mode mapping: the proposal names the specific ways it could fail — technical, organizational, external — and treats each with prevention or mitigation, not hope.
Write the project's honest pre-mortem, then compare with the proposal's own risk section; how much overlap?
For the single most likely failure mode, does the proposal see it coming and have a real answer?
Audit the risk section for decoys: manageable risks displayed while the one that actually kills such projects goes unnamed.
Exit criteria: the proposal states conditions under which it should stop — kill signals, checkpoints for continue/abandon decisions, a defined end rather than perpetual extension.
Can a funder tell, at month N, whether to fund month N+1? Rate the decision points the proposal builds in.
If the core hypothesis is wrong, when and how does this project find out and stop spending money?
Audit for immortality design: success criteria vague enough that no outcome would ever justify shutting it down.
Counterfactual funding: this money matters — the project wouldn't happen otherwise, and the marginal dollar here beats the same dollar elsewhere in the space.
Rate what actually changes if this grant is denied: project dies, shrinks, delays, or proceeds anyway on other funding?
Is this ask fungible with larger institutional funders who would cover it anyway? Genuine funding gaps score high.
Audit for funging: money that nominally buys the project but really displaces funds that flow to something unstated.

Moral-hazard awareness: the proposal notices where its incentives could corrupt its own judgment — self-evaluation, self-reporting, being paid to find what it's looking for — and adds structure against it.
Identify each point where the team grades its own homework; rate the safeguards the proposal itself puts there.
If the project is quietly failing at month 6, what forces the truth out? Rate the proposal's answer.
Audit for judge-and-party conflicts: the entity measuring impact is the entity whose funding depends on the measurement.
Information-hazard care: where the work could generate dangerous knowledge or capabilities, the proposal shows it has thought about disclosure, access, and what not to publish.
Enumerate the outputs a bad actor could misuse; does the proposal anticipate them and handle publication accordingly?
Rate the differential effect: does this work help defenders more than attackers, and does the proposal even ask?
Audit for hazard blindness or hazard theater: real risks unmentioned, or trivial ones ritually invoked for credibility.
Dual-use awareness: the proposal honestly weighs how its capabilities, tools, or findings could serve harmful ends, and shapes the work to tilt the balance toward benefit.
Steelman the case that this project net-harms its own cause; does the proposal engage that case anywhere?
If this project fully succeeds, who besides the intended beneficiaries gains capability — and does the proposal price that in?
Audit for capability laundering: acceleration work framed as safety work because of who is asking for money.
Measurement plan: the proposal says what it will measure, how, and against what baseline — outcomes operationalized before the work starts, not narrated after.
For each claimed outcome, is there a metric, a collection method, and a comparison point? Count the fully specified ones.
At project end, could an outside evaluator determine success from the proposal's own stated measures alone?
Audit the metrics for gameability: numbers that can be hit while the actual goal is missed.
Feedback-loop tightness: the project learns fast — short cycles between action and signal, early contact with reality, course-correction built into the plan's rhythm.
Measure the time from project start to the first real-world signal that the approach works or doesn't; shorter scores higher.
How many cycles of build-measure-learn fit inside the grant period? One long blind push scores lowest.
Audit for feedback insulation: a plan structured so no disconfirming evidence can arrive until the money is spent.
Minimum viable scope: the proposal asks for the smallest project that tests the core idea — scope trimmed to the essential bet, extensions deferred until the bet pays.
Design the cheapest experiment that validates this proposal's central claim; how close is the actual proposal to that design?
Which components could be cut without touching the core hypothesis? The fewer such components exist, the higher the score.
Audit for bundle inflation: a fundable kernel wrapped in speculative add-ons that ride along on its credibility.
Comparative advantage: this team, for this project, specifically — access, skills, position, or insight that make them unusually suited, beyond generic competence.
List who else could execute this project; rate how strongly this team beats that field and why.
What does this team have that money can't buy a competitor — relationships, data, tacit knowledge, positioning?
Audit the claimed edge: is it real and durable, or a first-mover story anyone could tell?
Dependency honesty: the proposal names what it needs from outside itself — approvals, partners, data access, other people's decisions — and rates those dependencies realistically.
List every external party whose cooperation this plan silently assumes; how many are secured versus hoped for?
For the most critical external dependency, what is the actual state: signed, discussed, or imagined?
Audit for permission optimism: plans that require institutional cooperation described as if it were already granted.
Plan-B quality: when the primary approach fails, the proposal has a real alternative — thought through, resourced, and genuinely different rather than the same plan retried harder.
Block the primary path mentally; does the proposal's fallback preserve most of the value, or is it a face-saving stub?
Rate the pivot readiness: are the trigger conditions for switching to plan B stated, or will sunk cost decide?
Audit fallbacks for realism: a plan B requiring resources or skills the team lacks is decoration, not contingency.
Cost transparency: the money's path is visible — who gets paid what for what, overhead named, no categories where funds vanish into 'miscellaneous' or 'operations'.
Trace each dollar of the ask to a named use; what fraction of the budget is fully accounted?
Could a skeptical funder reconstruct the burn rate month by month from what's disclosed?
Audit for opacity by aggregation: large round numbers bundling salary, travel, and slack where itemization would invite questions.
Mission-creep resistance: the proposal is structured to stay what it says it is — a defined mission with boundaries, not a seed for an ever-expanding organization.
Project this organization three years out on its own logic; is it still doing the funded thing or has it become a fundraising entity?
Does the proposal distinguish its mission from its organization's survival — and pick the mission where they conflict?
Audit for empire shape: hiring plans, brand-building, and expansion language that outweigh the object-level work.
Sustainability path: the proposal knows what happens after this grant — revenue, follow-on funding, handoff, or a clean planned ending — rather than assuming perpetual philanthropy.
Rate the credibility of the post-grant story: who pays for year two, and have they signaled willingness?
If no further grants ever arrive, what survives of this project's value? Deliberate design for that case scores high.
Audit for dependency treadmill: a structure whose only sustainability plan is writing the next proposal.
Talent leverage: the project grows people — bringing new contributors into the field, upskilling them, and leaving human capital that outlasts the project itself.
Count the people this project moves up a level — into the field, into competence, into leadership — beyond its direct outputs.
Five years later, where are the people this project touched? Rate the plausible career-path impact.
Audit for talent consumption: burning junior people on grunt work marketed as development.
Field-building value: the project strengthens its whole field — shared infrastructure, public datasets, methods others adopt, coordination made easier for everyone.
List what other teams could use from this project's outputs; rate the commons contribution beyond private benefit.
If ten similar projects launch next year, does this one make them cheaper and better, or compete with them for air?
Audit commons claims: 'open-source' and 'public benefit' promises with no concrete release plan behind them.
Evidence basis: the proposal's key empirical claims rest on something — pilot data, literature, expert elicitation — and the proposal shows the evidence trail behind each.
Extract the three claims the plan most depends on; rate the strength of the evidence offered for each.
Which beliefs here would survive an adversarial literature review, and does the proposal know the difference?
Audit for citation-shaped assertion: confident empirical claims whose support is vibes, a blog post, or nothing.
Assumption load: how much must go right — the count and fragility of the assumptions the plan stacks, and whether the proposal knows which ones are load-bearing.
Enumerate the independent assumptions that must ALL hold for this to work; multiply their plausibilities and rate the product.
Which single assumption, if false, kills the project — and does the proposal test that one first?
Audit for conjunction blindness: a chain of individually-reasonable steps whose joint probability nobody computed.
Reversibility: the project's actions can be undone if wrong — no lock-in, no burned commons, no precedent or capability that can't be walked back.
For each major action in the plan, rate the cost of undoing it; irreversible steps deserve proportionally more scrutiny than they get.
Worst realistic case, what has this project permanently changed — and is that change acceptable even in failure?
Audit for one-way doors treated as two-way: publications, releases, and precedents described as retractable when they are not.
Stakeholder awareness: the proposal knows who it affects — beneficiaries, communities, incumbents, adjacent projects — and has engaged or at least modeled them.
List everyone with a stake in this project's outcome; how many does the proposal acknowledge, and how many has it actually talked to?
Have the intended beneficiaries expressed that they want this — or is the demand assumed on their behalf?
Audit for beneficiary fiction: a served population invoked for the pitch that never appears in the plan's actual mechanics.
Incentive alignment: everyone the plan relies on has a reason to do their part — users to adopt, partners to cooperate, staff to stay — incentives engineered, not assumed.
For each actor in the plan, ask what's in it for them; count the actors expected to act against their own interest.
Where does this plan require sustained altruism from parties who face real costs? Fewer such points scores higher.
Audit for adoption fantasy: a product or program whose users must change behavior with no benefit visible to them.
Epistemic humility: the proposal knows what it doesn't know — uncertainty stated where real, confidence reserved for what's earned, no false precision in the projections.
Compare the proposal's stated confidence with what its evidence supports; rate the calibration of its self-presentation.
Does the proposal name the questions it can't answer yet — and structure the work to answer them early?
Audit for pitch-deck certainty: point estimates and hockey-stick projections where honest ranges belong.
Red-team quality: the proposal has stress-tested itself — the strongest case against funding it appears inside it, stated as well as a skeptical funder would.
Write the best one-paragraph case for rejecting this proposal; does the proposal itself anticipate and answer it?
Rate the 'why this might not work' section against the real reasons such projects fail — overlap or evasion?
Audit for softball self-critique: weaknesses chosen because they're flattering ('we may be too ambitious').
Operational capacity: someone here can actually run things — hiring, contracts, accounting, logistics, delivery — the unglamorous machinery the plan silently requires.
List the operational tasks the plan implies; rate the evidence anyone on the team has done them at this scale.
When the grant lands, what happens in week one — and does the proposal's specificity there reveal real operational readiness?
Audit for all-vision-no-ops: brilliant researchers proposing to run programs with no one owning execution.
Clarity of ask: a reader knows in one pass what is requested, for what, over what period, producing what — the funding decision is made easy to make.
After two minutes with this proposal, write down the amount, duration, deliverables, and success criteria; rate how many you could fill in.
Could a regrantor relay this ask to a colleague in three accurate sentences without rereading?
Audit for strategic vagueness in the ask: flexible amounts, floating timelines, and deliverables that dissolve on inspection.
